analysis.body:
According to the GAO, twenty of twenty-three federal agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, with three agencies reporting no AI applications. Agency use cases included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing drone photographs, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number of AI use cases. Most reported use cases were in the planning phase rather than production, though about 200 instances represented AI currently in use across the government.

The state of federal AI governance remains incomplete. The GAO found that five of twenty agencies provided comprehensive information for their reported AI use cases, while fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, including missing required elements such as AI life cycle stage or releasability status. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected AI requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing the AI Center of Excellence. However, the Offices of Management and Budget and Personnel Management did not fully implement selected requirements, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements.

Compliance across the federal system remains uneven. Ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from requirements. Without accurate inventories and government-wide guidance on AI acquisition and use, the GAO concluded that agencies cannot consistently manage AI or effectively address its risks and benefits.

The regulatory landscape is expanding rapidly. Per the tracking on this site, 5,260 AI bills are tracked across 53 U.S. jurisdictions and updated daily from LegiScan. International frameworks are also developing, with OECD.AI providing access to over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, and the GPAI initiative joining forces with OECD member countries' AI work in July 2024. Stanford HAI's AI Index measures government AI adoption and policy execution as part of its cross-sector analysis recognized globally by major media and high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

For government entities evaluating AI deployment, the evidence suggests both opportunity and caution. Federal agencies can use AI to analyze large datasets and visual information from sensors and drones, improving operational capabilities. However, the fragmented implementation record across agencies, incomplete data standards, and absence of government-wide acquisition guidance indicate that successful deployment requires strong internal governance, clear inventory practices, and compliance infrastructure before systems go into production. The concentration of early use cases at agencies like NASA and Commerce suggests learning from these implementations could guide deployment elsewhere in government.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports that there are 4,960 AI bills tracked across 53 US jurisdictions, with updates taken daily from LegiScan. It also notes that Stephen R. Jordan has published the “The Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page lists several AI-related audit and assessment services, including the AI Business Enablement Audit, AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, AI Risk & Governance Review, AI Efficiency & Process Optimization, AI IT Security Audit, AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy, Secure by Design in the Age of AI, and the AI Lawyer.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
